column2: Act Four
The Bronze City

The new map immediately appeared on the main screen. After a brief silence, everyone whipped around to stare at Lu Mingfei. Once the map had been deciphered, understanding it was simple. Everyone recognized the answer was correct.
The control room was deathly quiet. Beneath that stillness lay immense astonishment and unease, like a depth charge sinking silently through dark water.
For the first time, Lu Mingfei saw the petite girl’s face, translucent as ice and snow, and just as cold.
“Hello, panda!” Nono said solemnly.

With two enormous dark circles under his eyes, Lu Mingfei blundered into the second-floor classroom in the library. The first thing he saw was a pair of long, jean-clad legs swinging beside the lectern, ending in familiar purple-and-gold Mary Janes. Nono sat on the lectern, pointing at his nose.
He hadn’t expected her to speak to him voluntarily again, and excitement stirred in his heart. “Sorry, sorry. I don’t know how I ended up blowing away your boyfriend yesterday.”
Hisses immediately rose around the classroom. Only then did he remember what a tactless thing that was to say.
“Why apologize to me for blowing him away?” Nono shrugged. “Go to your seat. We’re about to start. Professor Manstein from the Disciplinary Committee is proctoring. I’m collecting the papers.”
Professor Manstein stepped out from the side, swept Lu Mingfei with a cold glance, and checked his watch. “Everyone is here. Now, the exam rules!”

“Cheating is absolutely forbidden. Offenders will be disqualified entirely! Don’t try to look at someone else’s paper. Cameras cover the whole classroom without a single blind spot! Don’t try to bring electronic communications equipment either. Radio signals in this room are monitored! I know you’re all geniuses, but greater geniuses than you have taken exams here. Every method of cheating you can think of has already been tried…” He spoke with ringing emphasis and tremendous authority.
Every desk had a nameplate. Lu Mingfei’s read RICARDO M. LU.

He paused, realizing this was now his official English name. Looking up, he saw Nono with her arms folded, head turned, gazing out the window in utter boredom. She must have arranged the nameplates. She had been the first person in the world to call him Ricardo, a name she had invented offhand. A very willful girl: once she called him Ricardo, Ricardo he remained.

He looked outside, too, and suddenly noticed the lovely weather. The morning sun had climbed above the clouds, its light spreading down along them to cast window shadows across the walnut desks. A faint crimson glow suffused the room.
Something stirred gently in his heart. Perhaps the fine weather had dispelled his mood. Perhaps it was having an official English name for the first time.
“Ricardo, then,” he told himself.
This was his first official day at Cassell, and it seemed a good omen. Suddenly he felt he might manage here after all. He couldn’t help grinning.

Remembering that he knew nothing about his fellow freshmen, he craned his neck to look around. They seemed to come from all over the world, different skin colors and faces in identical Cassell uniforms. Quite a few pretty girls made a pleasing sight.

“I’m Kiran, president of the Freshman Association. Delighted to meet you, Lu Mingfei. Our S-rank! May I have your autograph?” The boy on his right turned to shake hands. He looked Indian, handsome, with black curls and sharply contrasted black-and-white eyes, like a star in a Bollywood musical.
“Me?” It was the first time anyone had asked for his autograph. He felt both pleased and shy. “My handwriting’s terrible.”
Kiran passed him a pen and notebook. Unable to refuse such enthusiasm, Lu Mingfei left his turtle-crawl scrawl on the page.
“We’d like to invite you into the Freshman Association. We…”

“Gentlemen, this isn’t the time to socialize. Fail the 3E exam, and you won’t need a social circle here.” Manstein interrupted Kiran. “Before we begin, switch off your phones and place them at the corner of your desk with your student IDs.”

Shutdown tones sounded across the room. Only Lu Mingfei had nothing to do. In eighteen years, he had briefly owned just one N96. He stole looks at the others’ phones, feeling inferior, and considered spending some scholarship money on one if he actually passed. Then an almost translucent hand reached out ahead of him and pushed an expensive Vertu to a desk’s edge.
It was the first time he had seen one of those handmade luxury phones in person. They cost tens of thousands of yuan at least. He wanted another look, but its owner drew his gaze away.

A petite girl sat in the corner with her back to him, her skin coldly white. Having removed her uniform jacket, she wore a low-necked white T-shirt. Her blond hair, so pale it was almost white, had been braided and coiled into a bun, exposing a slender neck. Her entire figure was spare and pure as an ice sculpture.
His heart gave a jump. She seemed familiar. Yet he knew he couldn’t possibly know a girl like that. He could count the blond girls he had seen before turning eighteen on his fingers.

Black shutters slid silently from between the layers of the carved wooden window frames, sealing every window. Wall lamps came on. Nono walked down the aisles, giving each freshman several A4-sized sheets and a sharpened pencil.
The exam papers were blank.
Sharp breaths sounded around him. Nobody had expected blank papers. Someone raised a hand.

“No need to question it. There’s nothing wrong with your papers. I’ll be outside if you have questions. Discussion isn’t forbidden, provided you don’t copy someone else’s answers,” Manstein said. “Good luck.”

He and Nono left. As the door closed, students looked around and whispered, fidgeting like ants on a hot pan, their faces showing the shock of seeing ghosts in broad daylight. They couldn’t copy anyone’s answers. With no questions, where would answers come from?
Then, incredibly, the PA began blasting rock music: Michael Jackson’s “Beat It.”
The students stared at one another, completely dumbfounded.
One exception: Lu Mingfei. He had victory in hand.

“They’ll use strongly rhythmic music to cover the Draconic. Concentrate on a secondary melody in the lower register. That’s the incantation. Resonance gives the others spirit vision, so they may act strangely. Don’t panic. No resonance, no visions, no problem. Just listen carefully and copy the answers I gave you.” Fingel’s words were coming true.

He stealthily rolled up a sleeve. Eight tiny pictures drawn in ballpoint marched along his arm: the eight answers. The abstract pictures had proved too hard to memorize, forcing him to make a cheat sheet. The oldest methods worked best against high-tech proctoring. He could pretend to scratch, shielding his arm from the cameras with his body. Destroying the evidence was quick, too: spit in his palm and scrub. He had learned this from Su Xiaoqiang, the Little Celestial Princess, who copied notes onto her thighs and wore a short skirt to exams. Proctors knew where the notes were, but lacked the nerve to expose them.
Pricking those slightly mobile ears, he indeed heard someone chanting softly beneath Michael Jackson’s high, bright voice. It sounded like a curse, or a sacred hymn.
“Yanling: Prophet.” Halfway through, he recognized it and immediately began drawing.
“No wonder you’re the only S-rank freshman. Your composure proves your ability again,” Kiran said beside him. “I have no idea what to do. Perhaps I won’t pass. If so, I have a favor to ask.”
“No, no. I’m just drawing ducks.” Lu Mingfei tried to cover himself. The first answer really did resemble countless little ducks fitted together.
“I hope you’ll lead the Freshman Association.” Kiran ignored the ducks entirely.
“Lead?” The idea seemed to have nothing to do with Lu Mingfei.

“Lionheart and the Student Council are recruiting freshmen. But we shouldn’t be scattered. I’ve always believed we can bring something new to this campus. We only lack a leader like Caesar or Chu Zihang. I’m not capable enough. You are!”

“Could you not suddenly look like you’re entrusting me with an orphan? You make me feel like you’re Liu Bei in White Emperor City and I’m Zhuge Liang. I’m just an extra!” Lu Mingfei waved his hands. What did bringing something new have to do with him?
Kiran fell silent. Disappointment appeared in his eyes. Tears welled and slid down without a sound.

Lu Mingfei’s heart lurched. “Bro, don’t cry. We can talk… I know Liu Bei cried until Zhuge Liang came out of seclusion, but don’t just rush in crying… I’m trying to tell you Zhuge Liang lives next door. I’m really just an extra.”
“So… that’s how it is.” Still crying, Kiran smiled faintly.
“Finally, you understand. Good day to you, then,” Lu Mingfei said.

Kiran wiped his tears. A heavy sorrow that seemed to pierce time filled his clear eyes. Ignoring Lu Mingfei now, he bent to sketch on the white paper. His pencil whispered, twisted lines growing like a forest. He sobbed softly while drawing without pause. Anyone unaware might have thought he was writing his last will.
“He hasn’t understood. He’s… having spirit vision!” Lu Mingfei realized and looked around.

The whispering had stopped. An eerie atmosphere filled the room. Some students sat blankly, as though their entire families had just died. Others dragged their feet along the aisles, eyes empty, like Qu Yuan beside the Miluo River or some other walking dead. A girl leaped onto the platform and wrote and drew across the whiteboard in sweeping strokes, unaware her marker had long run dry. Another, a charming girl, cried “Hallelujah!” and danced in delight. Clearly trained, she moved beautifully. The chilling part was that this wasn’t a solo. An absent man seemed to hold her hand and dance with her, and she cast loving looks toward that invisible partner.
A whole room of demons danced, each absorbed, none disturbing another. Watching, Lu Mingfei broke into a cold sweat.
The world had gone mad without taking him along.
There was one exception: the ice-sculpture girl. Amid the revelry, she alone sat quietly, back straight as slender bamboo, as normal as he was.
Strangely normal.
“Judging by the time, resonance should have begun?” Outside, Masashi Toyama clutched his medical case, visibly nervous. “I’m ready. If the mental shock becomes too severe, I can go in immediately.”
“They should manage. This group seems quite capable,” Manstein said. “Nono, I remember how calm you were during your 3E exam. Spirit vision seemed nothing new to you.”
“My first spirit vision was when I was very young. By the exam, I was used to it,” she said.
“What was the first one?”
“My mother lay in bed. A shadow came and drew out her soul. She died.”
“Oh? Visions that realistic are rare. Most people only see confused lines and indescribable faces.” Manstein sounded curious.
“More realistic than you think. I didn’t only see someone take my mother’s soul… I saw his face.” Leaning against the wall, Nono looked toward the far end of the corridor and spoke quietly.
“Concentrate, concentrate! Almost there!” Lu Mingfei had finished seven questions.
Fingel had proved an excellent crooked merchant. Cassell really had dug up the exam from eight years before, changed the order, and used it again.

Beside him, who knew how many answers Kiran had finished? Smiling through tears, he kept sorrowfully recounting his tragic family history. He had been born in a Queensland slum. His father, an Indian doctor and alcoholic, often beat him and his mother. His poor grandmother planted a pomegranate tree behind the house, but died before its fruit ripened.
Lu Mingfei found it maddening, but the Freshman Association president’s feelings were too sincere to interrupt.

He completed the eighth answer, responding vaguely to Kiran while stealing a look at the girl. He could hardly believe there was another normal person here. Had a second fake dragon-blood descendant slipped in?

Someone sat on the desk behind her, watching him: a well-behaved-looking boy swinging his legs, in white square-toed shoes, a little black suit, and a white silk neck scarf. His golden eyes were pale.
Why was he here? Lu Mingfei was alarmed. The boy who haunted him like a restless ghost had returned. How had he entered the exam room? Or had he been among the students all along?

The boy beckoned slowly, smiling faintly like an angel. Afternoon sunlight shone behind him, casting his long shadow all the way onto Lu Mingfei. Feeling he could not refuse, Lu Mingfei pushed aside his desk, approached step by step, and finally took his hand. The boy hopped lightly down and led him to the window. It was like a man and woman in a courtly dance. Lu Mingfei felt he was dancing the woman’s part; the boy controlled their rhythm.

The boy vaulted lightly onto the sill, dangling his legs outside. Puzzled, Lu Mingfei sat beside him and studied him in the setting sun. He had never seen an older boy so pretty: a rounded face, an innocence between boy and girl, every movement gentle, an inborn elegance as though he had never trodden on dust. Leaning against the vine-covered frame, he gazed into the distance. Sunset gave his golden eyes a faint red glow, nothing like the cold severity of Chu Zihang’s.
The stillness felt too precious to break. Cassell in the sunset resembled an oil painting.
“Hey. I’m Lu Mingfei.” After much thought, he decided he ought to say hello.
“I’m Lu Mingze.” Looking into the distance, the boy spoke softly.

Lu Mingfei thought he was joking. He knew Lu Mingze best: his cousin, their shared bedroom, the same high school. Cute as a little boy, but now 160 centimeters and 160 jin, his face covered with adolescent acne. Unable to find a girlfriend at school, he posted despairing, sentimental sentences online to pick up girls. The boy before him was worlds apart. Not the slightest resemblance.
“Sunset? You’re online?” The boy turned toward him.
Lu Mingfei almost jumped. Sunset’s Imprint was his girl-impersonating QQ name, the account he used to tease his cousin. Every time he logged on, Lu Mingze said exactly that: “Sunset? You’re online?”

A simple greeting. Whenever his cousin typed it, Lu Mingfei sensed eager, lustful anticipation. From this boy, the same words felt utterly different. As though he had known Lu Mingfei would come—to that place, at that moment.
“Who are you really?” His voice trembled a little.

“Unimportant. This is your spirit vision. Everyone’s is different, but everyone sees what matters most deep in their heart. You saw me.” The boy calling himself Lu Mingze said, “I’m the person you care about most. An honor.”
“Stop joking. Isn’t spirit vision supposed to be… tangled lines? Look at you. Where’s the tangle? Not even a hair out of place!”

“You summoned me this time. Ask yourself why you see me. Everyone else is sad. Aren’t you?” Lu Mingze glanced at the sorrowful and joyful people in the classroom. On the sill, the two resembled spectators at a surrealist play.
“I don’t feel anything. If real spirit vision makes people sad, why don’t you look sad at all?”
“They truly are sad. They see the deepest things in their hearts. Where’s the deepest part of yours?” Lu Mingze extended a finger and poked his chest.
“Deeper than the heart… That’d be the stomach.” He couldn’t resist a lousy joke.
“Humans are stupid things. You, too. The only difference is that you deliberately make yourself stupid,” Lu Mingze said mildly. “You aren’t sad because I’m sad for you. Cruel, isn’t it?”
He smiled at Lu Mingfei, brilliantly in the sunlight.
“Are we… having a deeply emotional discussion of love between two males? ‘I’m sad for you’… Don’t you think your lines are straight out of a romance?” Gooseflesh rose all over Lu Mingfei.
Lu Mingze ignored him and stared at the sinking sun. In the final light, two lines of tears slipped silently down his face.

Lu Mingfei felt a hand squeeze his heart. Now he sensed the boy’s immense grief, like freezing water bursting forth, sweeping toward him to drown him. This was no romance, no affected pose. The boy’s sorrow was fierce, overwhelming, imperious. It inspired awe.
“Now I hate having you beside me.” Lu Mingze suddenly kicked him.

He lost his balance and fell. With a shock, he saw that he hadn’t been sitting at a second-floor library window, but atop an obelisk. Below lay no green Cassell lawn, only fanglike rocks that would tear him apart. He flailed for something to grasp, finding nothing but air.
Above, Lu Mingze stood silently on the obelisk’s spear-point summit, a giant sunset behind him, and waved goodbye. His beautiful face was expressionless.

Lightning seemed to flash through Lu Mingfei’s mind. A terrible image flickered: a night of bitter wind and rain, cold stone edging a flower bed, drops falling from leaves overhead. He and that boy—or his cousin Lu Mingze—sat in the darkness, holding each other tightly.
“Oh God! I don’t like men…” He fell into darkness.

He leaped from his chair, drenched in cold sweat, as though breaking through a dark membrane into reality. Nono stood before him, slapping his head hard enough to make him dizzy. They were alone in the empty exam room.
“Impressive. Sleeping that soundly during 3E,” she said. “Were you born in the Year of the Pig?”
“The Sheep… Exam over?” He rubbed his eyes.
“Almost lunchtime. The exam only lasts three hours.”
Startled, he saw burly maintenance men at the front removing the whiteboard covered in tangled lines and carrying the whole thing away.

Nono looked back. “Oh. She answered on the board. Nothing for it but to take it down and submit it. Emotions aren’t very stable during 3E. These accidents happen. But you were amazingly calm. We’re all curious. On the monitors, you quietly finished, put your head down, and snored. Even Manstein was impressed.”
“I… didn’t do anything strange?”
“Nothing. Like I said, amazingly calm.”

He pressed his forehead. When had that strange dream begun? When Kiran started crying? When he finished the paper? Or was he still dreaming? He hated not distinguishing reality from illusion. He pinched and twisted his wrist hard—accidentally too hard, bringing tears to his eyes.
“It’s swelling…” Nono pointed.
“Ow… I know…” He grimaced.
“Hand it in. You’re the last.”
“Oh, right.” He turned over the facedown “artwork” and passed it across.
“Let me count.” She checked the sheets, then snapped a stapler. “Nine pages. All together now.”

His head buzzed. Nine pages? Why nine? He clearly remembered drawing only eight childish sketches. There were only eight he could draw. Fingel had sold him eight answers. Where had the ninth come from?
“Wait, wait… Let me check.” He hurriedly reached for her stack.
“What’s to check? An S-rank like you can breeze through this.” She pulled it away.
In that brief instant, he saw his final sheet, the one absent from his memory. Undoubtedly his drawing. Yet it struck him like five bolts of thunder.
Dazed, he watched Nono pass it to Manstein, who dropped it into a black combination case. The lid snapped shut. Everything was settled. Lu Mingfei had no right to change it now.
Manstein scrambled the combination and handed the case to Nono. “Take it to Norma for marking.”
Pale, Lu Mingfei pressed his forehead. “Impossible… Could I… draw that well?”
At the dining table, he looked as though both his parents had died.
“Hey! Hey! How’d it go? That face… Caught cheating?” Fingel nudged him with a shoulder. “Don’t give me up!”
“Bullshit. What do you take me for? I’m an old hand!” He waved impatiently. “Answered all eight. Nobody saw my tricks. Afterward… I scribbled something else.”
“Fine, fine. As long as you didn’t write nonsense. Random scribbles get ignored.” Fingel relaxed.
“No nonsense… As a picture, it was better than anything I’ve ever drawn…” He didn’t know how to explain.

At lunchtime, they sat beneath the dining hall’s arched dome. The hall resembled a sanctuary from the age of knights. An enormous tree-shaped chandelier hung at its center, each leaf a small crystal lamp. Latin words welcoming freshmen adorned the granite walls. Students in dark-green uniforms gathered around tables. Each table’s student supervisor sat at its head. Fingel occupied that seat.
“Never knew you were a class officer, Brother Useless.”
“Just table captain. No place for eighth-year students, so they exiled me to the freshmen.”
“Pass these along.” A waiter placed a lunch before Fingel.
“The same menu?” Fingel sighed. “Freshman welcome lunch. Anything besides roast pork knuckle, mashed potatoes, and sauerkraut? I’ve eaten this eight times.”
“No problem. I can adjust it,” the waiter said.
“Something to look forward to? Beef in red wine?” Fingel’s eyes shone.
“I can offer roast pork knuckle with two portions of mashed potatoes, or roast pork knuckle with two portions of sauerkraut. Which would you prefer?”
“Got a pork knuckle wedged sideways in your skull?” Fingel inspected his head.
“Eat. You don’t get a choice. The menu’s a tradition, too. German food’s your home cooking, isn’t it? How can you not love it?”
“Cows back home make cow dung. I don’t like cow dung either,” Fingel said. “Understand the logic?”
“Why always German food?” Lu Mingfei prodded the knuckle, unsure where to start.

“Cassell’s a German family name. History’s most famous dragon-slaying clan. Every generation had a few experts. Supposedly, even the principal was only a second-string member back then,” Fingel said. “They’re the college’s leading board member, hence the German style.”
“The principal’s surname is Cassell?”
“No. The Cassells are all dead.”
“All dead?”

“Think what they did for a living all those years. Lasting into the twentieth century was lucky.” Fingel bit into his knuckle. “Anyway, exam’s over. Relax and wait. Classes should start tomorrow. Your Magic-Powered Mechanical Design I professor is Mans Rundstedt. Exam fanatic. Takes attendance every class. Watch out.”
“Eight in the morning! No sleeping in?” Lu Mingfei sighed.

“Attention, freshmen. Tomorrow morning’s Magic-Powered Mechanical Design I class is canceled. Professor Rundstedt will email the first chapter’s lecture notes to you.” Norma’s voice echoed through the hall.
“So thoughtful!” Lu Mingfei beamed.
“Rundstedt must be on assignment in China.” Fingel kept eating without looking up.
“On assignment?”
“Classes often stop for weeks because professors are away. Many work part-time for the Executive Department,” Fingel said. “Secret assignments.”
“Could it be…” Lu Mingfei started.
“Dragons. Canceling class at short notice means they’ve found a clue.”
Late at night, the tug Moniach shuddered in a storm on the upper Yangtze.
Such rain was rare in autumn. Water poured down, winds reaching force five. Other vessels had sheltered along shore. Only Moniach’s xenon lights flickered through rain above the uneasy water.

Professor Mans Rundstedt, also the captain, stood at the wheelhouse window. Rain slammed against the glass and burst apart. Wind howled; the boat rocked. Mans stood steady, smoking a cigar, waiting for news.
A baby’s cries drifted from the aft cabin. Mans frowned. “See what’s wrong with the little one. Always crying. Doesn’t anyone know how to look after a baby?”

“Professor, none of the Executive Department’s core personnel are married. Where do you expect us to learn?” The girl at the monitor never looked up. About twenty-three or twenty-four, she had black hair and a classically beautiful Latin face, and wore Cassell’s custom combat uniform.

“Call me Captain. I’m Moniach’s captain now, not your substitute lecturer.” He exhaled cigar smoke. “Stay at your posts. Since I’m the only married man, I’ll see to our dear baby. Selma, watch their vital signs. Any abnormality, haul in the lines!” “Understood!” the Latin girl replied.

“Captain, Yangtze Navigation Maritime Bureau advisory. The storm will continue after midnight. Winds rising to force ten, rainfall two hundred millimeters. Exceptionally severe, possible thunderstorms. They’re arranging rescue helicopters and advise abandoning ship.” The third officer removed his headphones.

“Tell them our draft is deep, the vessel is stable, and we can ride it out. We have patients aboard who shouldn’t abandon ship,” Mans said. “And don’t worry. This is Moniach. Not a tug, a warship. Force twelve is no problem.” He looked up at the black sky. After a silence, he murmured, “But this rain recalls Greenland’s icy sea ten years ago… Every time we approach these things, it feels like disaster is coming.”
He went aft. The forward cabin was quiet. Everyone had been rigorously trained at Cassell. Eyes on screens, they worked swiftly and silently.
Two intertwined heartbeats sounded through the headphones. On Selma’s monitor, rising and falling green points showed that two young, strong hearts still beat normally.
Fifty meters below the surface.
Fifty meters below the surface.
The spotlight penetrated only a short distance through deep water, a single blue-gray band. Aki Sakatoku’s slim figure floated nearby, close enough for Ye Sheng to reach out and take her hand.

Ye Sheng and Aki Sakatoku. Their twenty-seventh underwater operation together. Classmates at Cassell, they had joined the Executive Department at the same time. Diving partners for five years, they could read each other’s thoughts in a glance.
“I hear that S-rank freshman, Lu Mingfei, took out Caesar and Chu on his first day, during Freedom Day,” Ye Sheng said. “Didn’t show that potential when we interviewed him.”
“Wonder how Nono persuaded him,” Aki said. “Usually talks nonsense, but sometimes she has plenty of ideas.”
A separate communications cable linked the two of them tightly.

Nono had indeed talked nonsense about one thing. Ye Sheng and Aki weren’t lovers. Regulations forbade it. Deep diving was dangerous: oxygen tanks and a layer of nanomaterial suit protected you from pressure equivalent to more than ten atmospheres, while a single cable connected you to the human world. Nerves could easily become overwrought. Romantic feelings between partners could lead to unpredictable results.

The department prohibited romance between underwater partners, saying violation of that rule had caused the terrible losses in Greenland’s icy sea ten years ago. No one knew what that operation had been. But nobody in the department today had taken part, permitting a rough conclusion: the team ten years ago had all died.

They reached the bottom. Fifty meters of water filtered the storm into gentle ripples. Before the Three Gorges Reservoir flooded it, this had been mountain country. Currents had worn the rocks smooth, making footing difficult. Ye Sheng extended steel claws from his fins, settled lightly on a rock, and felt through the sediment.
He showed Aki his find: a pottery shard bearing an ancient design.
Examining it, she said, “At least a thousand years old. Before Central Plains culture absorbed Shu culture. Perhaps a relic of White Emperor City.”
“Not much oxygen left. Is this the intended location? I don’t see the supposed ruins of White Emperor City.” She looked around. Nothing in sight resembled a city.
“Norma, I need a sonar terrain scan,” Ye Sheng called.
“Understood. Preparing sonar scan.” Far away in America, the central processor answered at once.
A three-dimensional sonar image outlined in dark-green contours appeared on their helmet displays. Sound was far more useful than light underwater.

“We can’t see it,” Ye Sheng pointed, “but mountains lie northeast and southeast. Above water is Baidi Mountain; below, Chijia Mountain. They form a gate. Opposite is the old Caotang River, through a valley. In Chinese feng shui, this is where the mountain dragon and water dragon meet, gathering yin and yang. An excellent place for a city. The ruins may be here. We need the entrance.”
“After a thousand years, any entrance will be under meters of soil.” Aki laughed softly. “To save time, I’ll have to trouble you. Please.”
“It leaves me exhausted every time,” he complained. “I need an anchor.”
“Haven’t I always been your anchor?” She swam behind him, extended the claws in her fins to grip the rock, and wrapped both arms around his waist.
An unspoken understanding. When Ye Sheng sent out his Snakes, he was helpless as an infant. A current could carry him away, or a tangled cable endanger his life. So Aki always held him this way.
He closed his eyes. In spirit vision, restless snakes tangled in his mind, scales gleaming cold, hard blue-green. His body shuddered slightly.
Yanling: Snake.
He gave them an order. Released from deep in his mind, the snakes flowed through his limbs, then surged out and vanished into the water.
Moniach detected a powerful burst of bioelectricity at a point below the surface.

The Snakes were Ye Sheng’s Yanling and his helpers. Normally they slept deep in his mind. Only he could wake them. Like thousands of scouts, they explored his surroundings. Scientifically, they were a bioelectric current. To dragons, they were servants he had subdued.
In good conductors, the Snakes became many times stronger. The reservoir’s enormous water mass greatly amplified them. A domain five kilometers in radius lay under his watch.

His awareness followed them into every crevice, down and farther down. He opened his eyes, faint golden light flowing through them. Through the Snakes’ eyes, he saw a world made of countless tiny channels, joining and separating, extending without end. His Snakes traveled through them, gray mist spreading wherever they went.

Aki felt his body cooling. At his weakest now, his pulse fell to thirty beats a minute and his blood temperature dropped. Through the faceplate, his face looked ashen, only the unsettling pale-gold pupils shining. She held him tighter, trying to share her warmth. She always did. He led their team, but now he needed her protection.

“Captain! Maritime Bureau warns of a possible magnitude-five underwater earthquake!” the third officer shouted. “They insist on sending rescue helicopters. They may have realized something’s wrong here.”
Mans entered the forward cabin, bent beside Selma, and studied Ye Sheng’s pulse. “Stall a little longer. An earthquake is bad news. I have a feeling… we’re close. Very close.”

Ye Sheng shivered. The pale gold vanished, his pulse climbed rapidly, and his blood warmed again. Almost all the Snakes returned to sleep. One alone kept descending, piercing darkness—and finding light!
“A result?” Aki asked.
“A huge metal mass about forty meters beneath us. The Snake moves incredibly fast there. Only metal conducts that well.”
“Forty meters down? It’s solid rock. We can’t cut through forty meters of it. Dragon King Norton couldn’t have put his palace inside rock.”
“Ye Sheng, Aki. Prepare to surface,” Mans’s voice sounded. “Possible magnitude-five underwater earthquake tonight. It’s dangerous down there.”

“Understood. Aborting for now.” Then Ye Sheng’s expression changed. The water around them was shaking. Aki felt it, too. Tremors came through the rock she stood on. The entire bottom shook. Rising sediment obscured their view.
“It’s begun… Damn! Their warning was far too accurate this time!” From the sonar, Mans saw exactly what was happening. He turned to the first officer. “Reel in! Reel in! Pull them up!”

The winch turned, drawing in the black cable that served as communications line and lifeline. Then a snapping sound reached him through the storm. The winch raced out of control. His face changed. With no tension on it, the machine was running free. The lifeline had broken.
In the turbid water, the spotlight was no brighter than a firefly, barely illuminating two pale faces. Ye Sheng could only hold Aki tightly. They were falling fast.

A clear crack had raced toward them from afar, like an invisible blade slicing rock. The layer, meters thick, split and sank. Before they could react to the bottom tearing open, tremendous pressure struck from above, like a wave tens of meters high crashing onto their heads.

Underwater, pressure came equally from every side. Only one thing could abruptly increase pressure from overhead: a great cavity opening below. Millions of tons of water poured into it, sweeping them and the broken rocks along. Not even a nanomaterial lifeline could resist such force.
The forward cabin fell silent. Mans thrust both hands into his hair and dragged them backward hard enough to hurt his scalp.

Distorted static hissed from the speakers. Signal lost, survival unknown. That lifeline had also been their sole communications channel. He might have lost his two finest students. He had always known it could happen. Something similar had happened ten years before.
With the situation below unknown, should he send a rescue party? Or abandon them, as in Greenland? He thought desperately.
“If you see a wall whose edge you can’t see above, below, left, or right, whose end you can never reach—what is it?” A calm voice sounded through the cabin.
Mans looked up in surprise. Ye Sheng.

“Death. Read that in a book once. Now I understand. This is Ye Sheng. Aki and I are alive. I’m speaking through the Snakes’ current. We’ve reached the palace of Norton, King of Bronze and Fire. Please respond.”
A special use of the Snakes: carrying Ye Sheng’s voice back and forth between the depths and Moniach like messengers.
“Confirmed?” Mans’s voice trembled slightly.
“Professor, if you saw the bronze wall in front of me, you’d believe it.”

Deep below, Ye Sheng and Aki held hands tightly, suspended in eerie green water. Above, the spotlight vanished into green gloom. Every direction looked the same, without end. Except ahead, where a huge bronze wall extended up, down, left, and right, seemingly boundless.
The earthquake had paused. Sediment settled, clearing the view.
Amid the verdigris, Ye Sheng made out a weathered design identical to the one on the pottery shard, only much larger: a face burning in flames.
“A city… of bronze?” Aki whispered. Their private communications cable still connected them.
“Like the one he supposedly cast on the ice and snow of northern Europe,” Ye Sheng said. “Lucky! Without the quake opening this fissure, we could never have drilled down here.”
“Yes. Who’d know it was buried dozens of meters underground? An entire city cast in bronze. How did they do it?”

“Professor von Schneider had a theory. Norton hollowed out a mountain for a mold and poured molten bronze in from the summit. As the city took shape, heat shattered the rock, producing something even modern technology can’t achieve: an entire bronze city. His home.”
“Insane to imagine,” Aki said softly. “Will he… be inside?”
“We’ll have to go in to find out. I look forward to it.”
“Ye Sheng, Aki, withdraw,” Mans said. “There may be aftershocks. And you’re low on oxygen.”

“Professor, know what I’m looking at? The border between the human and dragon worlds. If you touched the edge of the world, would you stop to catch your breath? If an aftershock buries this opening, you’ll regret it forever,” Ye Sheng said. “Something’s inside. I can feel it. The Snake that entered is circling something. It’s terrified.”

Mans stayed silent for a full minute. “Fear… Is it Norton’s own tomb that’s frightening the Snake?” He drew a deep breath. “All right. I understand. I’ll replace your equipment. But remember, two hours. Both oxygen and power will last only two hours. Maritime’s helicopters should arrive by then, too. At that point, we’ll be forced to halt.”
“Understood. But right now I’d love to know where the Dragon King’s front door is. Not a crack in this thing.”
“I think I know. Wait. I’ll bring a locksmith down shortly,” Mans said.
He went aft and called. “Principal, a development in Operation Kuimen. In a fissure opened by the earthquake, we’ve found a city cast entirely in bronze.”
A pause. “An ancient bronze city. The palace of Norton, King of Bronze and Fire.”
“We should explore immediately. Risky, with this storm on the Yangtze,” Mans said. “But we can hardly wait. We have competitors.”
“Competitors? Who? Few can compete with us in archaeological exploration.”

“An underwater expedition funded privately from Hong Kong. Exploring a newly discovered submerged tomb. They don’t seem to know anything about our affairs, but they’ll dive soon. If they find the bronze city, secrecy may become impossible.” Mans paused. “Ye Sheng senses something inside. It isn’t a dead city.”

“Understood. Approved,” the principal said. “Remember: never let a pureblood dragon escape our surveillance. Capture first, kill second. Let something like that out of our control, and the whole world will be overturned.”
“With limited time, may I use the Key to open the city?”
“This is exactly why I had you bring him!”

Mans put away his phone, bent over the cradle, and gently stroked the baby. The child, howling a moment before, was now quiet, gazing innocently around with wide eyes. A woman sat beside him, alluring, in her thirties or forties. A diamond ring on her left ring finger suggested a wealthy husband.
“Sweetheart, do you feel it?” Mans pinched the baby’s nose.
“Be careful using him. Our only Key. Such pure dragon blood—we may never find another. Not even Chu Zihang compares,” the woman said.
“Much better behaved than Chu, though.” Mans played with him. “Don’t look so distrustful. You’re only his foster mother. We all love the Key. Spend more time caring about your own daughter.”
“Chen Motong?” she said mildly. “I don’t see her treating me as a mother.”

“Your family problems are complicated… Better leave them out of work.” Carefully lifting the child, Mans met her eyes. “Forgive a word more, though. A mother who regards a daughter as her daughter only if the daughter first regards her as a mother—isn’t she asking too much? You have a beautiful foster daughter.”

“You’re her adviser. I know you care for her. But a girl who can watch her own mother die, then sit quietly for two days and nights without crying until the body collectors knock, doesn’t invite affection.” Her voice never wavered.
“All right.” Mans sighed. “I only mean that Nono can be odd… but she’s… a very good child.”
He returned forward and stood at the window, arms extended, waiting for Selma to fit his diving suit.
His gaze crossed the rain toward the distant mountain above water. “White Emperor City. I love that name.”
“Captain, is White Emperor City the Dragon King’s sleeping palace, or an actual city?” Selma asked.

“There is a city, founded more than two thousand years ago. It was above water until a few decades ago. The Three Gorges Reservoir submerged most of it. Only the White Emperor Temple remains on that island. Its founder, Gongsun Shu, rebelled against Wang Mang, an idealistic dynastic usurper, and established his own state here. Some called him the White Emperor.”
“Reminds me of the White King,” the third officer said.
“Not the White King. The King of Bronze and Fire, also called the Gray King. A noble first-generation dragon, one of the Four Monarchs. Norton. Born directly of the Black King Nidhogg.”
“By himself?” Selma asked. “So the Black King’s his… father or mother?”

“Current research says most dragons mate and have parents. First-generation dragons differ. The Four Monarchs weren’t born from male and female pairing. Representing the four elements, they split directly from the Black King. He is both father and mother,” Mans said. “Chinese elements are metal, wood, water, fire, and earth. Dragons have only earth, water, wind, and fire. You should have learned this in introductory alchemy.”
“So that Chinese man, Gongsun Shu, was a Dragon King?”

“No. Someone behind him. Before becoming emperor, Gongsun Shu claimed to see a dragon rise from a well and lie before his residence. Chinese histories record a ‘dragon appearing before the mansion hall.’ He took it as auspicious,” Mans said. “Sichuan lay in ancient China’s west. He thought his good fortune came from metal, whose color is white. Hence White Emperor. Not our White King: the name’s real meaning in Chinese is King of Metal. Coincidentally, Norton performed two miracles: unrivaled fire, and refining bronze from deep within the earth to use as weapons.”
“Why would this person… this dragon, do all that? Building a bronze city is an incredible undertaking!”

Mans spread his hands and removed his cigar. “We’ve never known. To understand their aims, first we must understand what dragons are and their relationship with humans. An academic puzzle. Fossils alone can’t answer it. We may have to capture a living Dragon King and question him.” He paused. “Tonight’s a chance!”
Ye Sheng sensed the Snake inside the city becoming more agitated, swimming much faster.

A spotlight shone down. A figure swam toward them. Mans tapped his faceplate in greeting, releasing bubbles. He resembled a woman nine months pregnant: a rigid transparent pouch projected from his suit, containing a baby in a tiny diving outfit. In depths that would frighten adults, the infant miraculously didn’t cry, only looked slowly around, faint golden light flowing in his eyes.
Mans brought new communications cables, connected them, and replaced the divers’ oxygen tanks.
“Whoa! The Key!” Ye Sheng patted his belly pouch to amuse the infant. “Professor, you look like a diving kangaroo.”
“Then you’re a fox trying to steal my joey! Remember, two hours.” Mans raised two fingers. “Get ready. I’m opening the door.”
Floating behind him, Ye Sheng and Aki each placed a hand on his shoulder. He crossed his arms over his chest and firmly patted his finest students’ hands.

He closed his eyes, pressed a hand to the bronze wall, and chanted quietly. Song and roar together, the immense sound pierced deep into their minds. Opening his eyes, he did something that would stop an ordinary diver’s heart: at a depth of a hundred twenty meters, he opened the faceplate of his pressurized suit. Crushing water pressure would act directly on his frail human body. Every bubble in his blood could race outward and rupture his vessels.
His voice boomed through the water. He released his Yanling.
Yanling: Dustless Realm.

Water swirled around him. A transparent shell expanded rapidly outward, forcing water from a sphere several meters across. Currents spun furiously around it. High-pressure oxygen escaping his tank filled the bubble. Incredibly, they stood in air!

Where his hand touched, a north wind seemed to scour the wall. Great sheets of verdigris flaked off, revealing fresh metal, black-green with an oily gleam. A design emerged clearly: a raised human face biting a burning stick. Strange—contorted with pain, yet refusing to unclench its teeth.
“Sweetheart, the rest is yours.” Hanging from the wall by steel claws, Mans carefully lifted the infant from his pouch.

Silence, broken only by the roaring vortex. The golden-eyed baby was quiet for a long time, then laboriously straightened to stand on Mans’s palm. Only a few months old, pacifier in his mouth, cow-patterned onesie on his body, sparse baby hair on his head. Yet he stood upright, solemn as a priest. Studying the face, he slowly reached out a chubby hand and touched one finger between its brows.

A bronze projection cut the tender finger. Blood spread over the suffering face. For an instant, Aki saw it twist with pleasure. Ye Sheng caught the falling pacifier. A deep, bell-like sound poured from the infant’s mouth. The wall began to resonate.

Blood streamed into the bronze mouth as though powerfully sucked away. The infant stood with a martyr’s indifference, showing no distress. He bent slightly, almost to kiss the mouth. Mans seized him, stopping the disturbing movement. Taking a hemostatic bandage, he carefully wound it around the little finger and patted his cheek. “Key, enough. You were wonderful.”

After drinking, the face was still, then slowly opened its mouth in a yawn. Horrible sounds of heated, cracking metal came from within. A black opening about a meter across appeared, edged above and below by the face’s teeth—not human teeth, but dagger-sharp fangs.
“The entrance,” Ye Sheng whispered.

“A great alchemical achievement. Spirit housed in the purest matter, serving as a guardian,” Mans said. “A living spirit. Only exceptionally pure dragon blood briefly satisfies it. About two hours. It will close the door.”
“About?” Ye Sheng asked. “That imprecise? On a Moon mission, could you say landing in about two hours? This is more dangerous than the Moon!”
“Save a minute of discussion, then,” Mans said. “I’ll end the Yanling. Once the passage floods, you can enter.”
The pale gold faded from the infant’s eyes. He raised his bandaged finger, looked at it in surprise, then burst into thunderous, utterly heartbroken wails.
“There, there, don’t cry. Poor sweetheart.” Looking like a helpless father, Mans put him back in the pouch.

“Remember. Two hours.” He looked into Ye Sheng’s eyes and repeated it. “Norton isn’t due to awaken yet. Find his egg. If you can’t secure it, destroy it.” He handed over a black metal box. “Alchemical equipment from Equipment. Destroys eggs. Get fifty meters clear before detonation.”

Ye Sheng gave a thumbs-up. Mans closed his helmet. The Yanling ended, and the air sphere instantly shattered into countless bubbles racing upward. Inrushing water nearly stopped the two divers’ breathing. Their professor, meanwhile, pushed off the bronze wall with fishlike agility, activated the hydraulic thruster on his back, and shot away.
Aki watched him fade into the distance. Darkness returned. The only light was Ye Sheng’s helmet spotlight.
Suddenly she felt cold—the annihilating cold at the edge of the world.
“Ye Sheng!” She turned.
“I’m here.” Smiling, he extended his hand and clasped hers through their thick gloves.
Mans climbed over the gunwale, removed his fins, and raced forward without even stripping off his suit.
“Vitals normal, signal clear. They’re deep inside. Bronze statues everywhere, passages like a space station, and… You wouldn’t believe it! God, nobody could without seeing!” Selma met him, excited.
“Main screen,” Mans said.

Dark-green video from the divers appeared. In the spotlight, shifting ripples played across an incredible bronze object. Circular, edged with sharp wolflike teeth. At first sight, you imagined throwing it, watching it howl through a strange arc, bite into an enemy’s neck, and spin.
“Incredible craftsmanship,” Mans murmured.
“Some kind of weapon,” Selma said.
“Not a weapon. A gear. Part of a system.”
The view pulled steadily back, apparently as Ye Sheng swam slowly away with his helmet camera. The lens rose above water.
“Plenty of air trapped inside. That buys time,” Mans said.
“No. Very little oxygen. Centuries sealed up—the metal’s oxidation consumed it,” the first officer said. “Their tanks still give only an hour thirty-five… No, thirty-three.”
A second disk entered view, then a third, a fourth… Countless disks covered a bronze wall tens of meters high, teeth meshing. Mans paused and looked at his wrist, at his mechanical Omega dive watch.
“Ye Sheng reporting live. I feel like I’m swimming inside a watch movement.”

“Alchemical machinery,” Mans said. “That complexity—Norton’s practically a mechanic. Not surprising, though. Ancient Chinese records mention wooden birds flying through the sky without landing. Fifty minutes left. Find the sleeping palace quickly.”
“Understood. The spot my Snake circles feels very close.”

He touched the black box and turned to Aki. “Photograph and sample here. I’ll find the Snake’s position, below us. Watch my vitals. If anything happens, don’t attempt rescue. Withdraw first. Team leader’s order.”
“Yes,” Aki said.

“You may be a stupid teammate, but at least you’re obedient.” He gave a thumbs-up and rolled underwater. The ancient city consisted of successive chambers joined by bronze passages. After flooding, most passages lay below the surface, like an anthill half submerged.

Aki shone her flashlight upward. The enormous chamber resembled a giant’s palace. Ancient patterns covered the dome: a huge tree’s spreading foliage, its leaves and branches curling into unreadable characters.
“Draconic?” She suddenly understood.
Taking out her waterproof camera, she divided the dome into sections and photographed them. Data immediately returned to Moniach.

“Back it up! Back it up! An unexpected bonus!” Mans rubbed his hands delightedly. For the first time since Nicolas Flamel, humanity had obtained such a wealth of Draconic. Though unreadable for now, to dragons, who transmitted power through writing, it was priceless.

Complex patterns kept entering her viewfinder. They recalled her spirit vision during 3E, but were more intricate. Leaves gathered into faces, then separated into ancient characters lost for years, turning counterclockwise across the dome. Wanting more photographs, she reduced her tank’s output pressure to extend her time while waiting for Ye Sheng.
Reduced oxygen made her dizzy. The patterns blurred. She paused, closed her eyes, and breathed deeply, trying to clear her head.
“Aki, your pulse is rising. Are you all right?” Selma’s voice was slightly tense.
“Fine. Just a little dizzy.”
She returned her folding knife to its pocket, opened her eyes, and swam toward the chamber’s edge.
“Signal lost!” Selma cried aboard Moniach. “Data link with Aki interrupted!”
Mans paused. “Reel in! Reel in! Warn Ye Sheng!”
The stern winch turned again, hauling in her lifeline.
“No tension.” Selma looked up, all color drained from her face. “Aki’s line has broken again!”
Ye Sheng surfaced beside Aki and supported her arm, making her feel much better.
“You’re back? Finished? I didn’t hear an explosion.” Seeing him relieved her greatly.
“Underwater blasts aren’t very loud,” he said. “Taken care of. Finish sampling, then we’ll head back. Not much time.”
“All right. Finished photographing the dome.”
“Take some bronze for analysis, too.” He pointed at a statue on the wall nearby. “We could bring that back. The image isn’t ancient Chinese. It comes from Europe.”
“Sure.” With Ye Sheng pulling her, she swam toward it. Water parted along her suit, carrying a strange hint of warmth.

The statue was only a few dozen centimeters tall, nothing like the life-sized figures at the entrance. Wearing ancient Chinese robes and holding an ivory ceremonial tablet, it stood on a bridge-shaped bronze rod. Its bowed head suggested aristocratic courtesy and respect. But the head was a cobra’s, its slender neck protruding incongruously from the collar.
A snake-faced man.
“What is it?” Aki turned to Ye Sheng.
“No idea. Some dragon totem, perhaps. Bringing it back will be useful anyway. Take it down.”

She nodded and swam over. Face-to-face with it, she felt a flicker of surprise. Its eyes were pure silver, flashing harshly against dark bronze, almost blinking. She reminded herself to dismiss strange thoughts. Only reflected light. Underwater work demanded calm.
Grasping its neck, she found it lighter than expected and lifted it easily.

A shadow suddenly rose beside her and reached for her throat with indescribable speed. Cassell’s physical training and years underwater took over. Without hesitation, she drew her folding knife and slashed.
“Ye Sheng! Watch out!” she shouted.
Ye Sheng carried a Russian SSP-1 underwater pistol modified by Equipment.

But the shadow moved faster than either of them. A weapon in its hand deflected her knife and struck her helmet hard. Instantly unable to fight back, she instinctively tumbled backward to avoid the next blow, only to find herself held tightly.
“Ye Sheng! Shoot!”
“Shoot whom?” the shadow asked.

She froze. Ye Sheng’s voice. During training on the Great Barrier Reef, her oxygen tank had once failed. At the brink of suffocation, hearing that voice had brought her back, saved her. Her eyes widened. Light inside the shadow’s helmet illuminated the face. Ye Sheng’s.
“Why are there two Ye Shengs?” Terror exploded inside her.

She turned. The Ye Sheng who had brought her here was gone. A life-sized snake-faced bronze statue floated there instead. Nobody knew how bronze could float. Silver-inlaid eyes gleamed, and its fanged mouth seemed to smile mockingly.
Ye Sheng drew his SSP-1 and blew its face off. “Came back and found you swimming here. That thing floated behind you. Don’t know why. Kept following until you reached out and activated the system.”

Only then did Aki discover her lifeline and data cable were severed. Feeling down the line, she found a perfectly smooth end. A blade had cut it. Touching her waist, she suddenly remembered… She herself had drawn her knife and cut the lifeline!
“My God!” She shuddered. “A hallucination?”
“Perhaps the Draconic.” Ye Sheng pointed at the dome. “Taking pictures in sequence amounted to reading it in a particular order. Induced spirit vision. Your mind wasn’t under your control.”
“That kind of spirit vision… Strange.”
A horrifying sound arose around them, like rusty sheets of iron being scraped together beside their ears, magnified hundreds or thousands of times.

They looked at the bronze walls. Tens of thousands of gears slowly began turning. A mighty bell rang through the chamber. Rust flaked from teeth that clattered together. Ye Sheng looked sharply up. High in unseen darkness, a huge bell of unprecedented design sounded, its bronze pendulum swinging around its bearing. The snake-faced figures on the walls moved together, raising ivory tablets, bending slender necks to look at the dome, like an ancient pilgrimage ritual.
“You activated the system.” Ye Sheng looked at the rod Aki had moved. “Don’t know what system, but it doesn’t look good… It’s a… trap!”

He felt a shock. The Snake left nearby on guard was fleeing. Unprecedented. His loyal servants always lived deep in his consciousness. Now immense terror drove one away from its master. His head hurt violently. Deep inside, the others swam in panic, as though trying to burst his skull.
Get out immediately. Instinct told him that.

Drawing Aki’s knife, he drove it between two gears. The force was extraordinary; the nanomaterial blade exceptionally sharp. It sank two inches into bronze. The gears jammed against it. The great bell’s motion immediately slowed, deprived of power.
“Every machine needs power. Alchemical machinery, too!” he shouted. “Move! The entire city… seems to be moving!”
The knife fell. Power returned to the great bronze bell. It pealed at full force.
Deafening bells. Lu Mingfei jolted awake and sat up, turning toward the window. Brilliant midday sun.
“Why the bells? Americans don’t nap?” His first reaction was to curse; his second, to pull the quilt over his head and go back to sleep.
Huddled beneath it, he realized something was wrong. The bells didn’t stop. Fingel napped, too, like a dead pig. Was he still asleep and swearing now? Lu Mingfei slowly lifted the quilt.
“Hi. Over here,” someone said by the window.
A boy in a little black suit, white silk shirt, and square-toed shoes sat on the sill, staring quietly into the distance.
Lu Mingze.
After hesitating, Lu Mingfei tiptoed behind him and suddenly mussed his hair. The touch was utterly real. Freshly washed hair, smooth and pleasant; real body warmth, too.
“Hey… Could you tell me if I’m dreaming?” He leaned beside the window.
“Depends what you mean by dreaming. By your definition, what you see now isn’t the real world.” The boy shrugged. “But what is? Perhaps your supposed real world is the dream.”

“It feels really, really, really real! Never had a dream this real.” He pointed at the clock tower. “Clock’s still running. Went to sleep at twelve, now it’s one-thirty. Everything’s normal except you. Without you, nothing would seem like a dream.”

“Don’t trust your eyes too much. Seeing doesn’t make it real. Perhaps you’re dead, only imagining you’re standing here talking.” The boy met his eyes. “Maggots are crawling through your corpse, happy as worms in cheese holes.”
He paused, suddenly cold. “Stop! Stop! I just had cheese tonight. Spare me the creepy comparisons. And don’t push me out this time. We can talk.”
“I won’t. You were just too annoying last time. Can’t stay long. Only here to remind you: things are happening. Be ready.”
“What things? Dragon invasion? End of the world? Anything less, don’t wake me from my nap.”
“Didn’t you hear? The bell has rung.” The boy spoke meaningfully. “Prepare. To keep studying here as an S-rank, you can’t be utterly useless. Remember StarCraft cheat codes?”
“Of course. power overwhelming is invincibility. show me the money gives ten thousand minerals and gas. black sheep wall reveals the map.” Familiar territory.
“Exactly. black sheep wall. Reveals the map. Useful, right?”
“Obviously. Don’t you know how important scouting is?”

“The first code I’ll teach you is black sheep wall. Now unlocked. Use it for a detailed map of your surroundings. But don’t overuse it. Too much, and you’ll be discovered.” The boy smiled mysteriously.
Lu Mingfei paused. “All this supernatural stuff. Think we’re in Harry Potter? A magic school? Just open my mouth and say… black…”
The boy suddenly covered his mouth, raising a finger and wagging it. “Told you. Don’t overuse it.”
Hopping off the sill, he patted Lu Mingfei’s shoulder. “Remember. black sheep wall. When you need it most… You’ll need it soon.”

Like a classmate dropping by, he opened the door and left. When it closed, deathly silence filled the room. Lu Mingfei stood stunned for a long time, shuddered hard, and pinched his face fiercely. Outside came a piercing alarm, as though some master thief had simultaneously triggered every bank alarm in the world.
“The kid’s not playing with a lighter under a fire alarm?” he thought.
He rushed out and shouted, “What kind of flying stunt are you pulling?”
“And you’re driving a tank!” someone replied.
He froze, seeing who stood before him. In her uniform skirt, Nono patted his face. “Wake up. Sleep scrambled your brains?”

He stood in the dormitory corridor. Red ceiling lights flashed; hidden wall speakers shrieked. Uniformed male and female students, all serious, converged from the stairways toward the elevators. Cassell was small, so Dormitory Area One was coed.
“A fire alarm? Does everyone have to look bereaved while evacuating?” He looked around.

“First thing after enrolling: read the Emergency Handbook. Since its foundation, Cassell’s stood ready for any dragon-related incident. This alarm means an unexpected emergency. High-ranking students assemble at the library. Hey, Nono! Prettier every day!” Fingel’s disheveled head poked from their room. Lu Mingfei knew he dared show only his head. He slept naked.
“Still sleeping naked, I see,” Nono said.

“An F-rank loser like you knows the whole handbook! What’s it for, anyway? Like Earthquake Survival?” Lu Mingfei asked. “Nothing to do with me, right? 3E results aren’t out. I shouldn’t count. Can I go back to bed?”

“More like Dragon-Slayer Reserve Training for Dummies: Your First Step onto the Battlefield. Actually, I wanted you to bring me a Coke on your way back,” Fingel said. “Back in my A-rank days, missing roll call in an emergency cost internship credits.”
“I haven’t even got internship credits!” Lu Mingfei cried.
“Come on!” Nono grabbed him and ran.
“Why drag me? Shouldn’t you drag your Caesar?” he stumbled along.
“Doesn’t need dragging. He loves this stuff. He’s surely gathered every Student Council elite and headed for the library already!”
A crowd rushed into the library’s main control room.

Before he caught his breath, Caesar strode in, uniformed, head high, expressionless. Equally expressionless council officers followed with briefcases, as though attending the Joint Chiefs of Staff. Chu was already there. The two societies had divided the high-ranking students between them, seated on opposite sides without mingling.

Lu Mingfei counted quietly. Thirteen students, all A-rank or higher. Outside the two societies were only himself, Kiran, and the petite ice-sculpture girl from 3E. She sat in front, showing everyone only her back. Professors occupied the other seats. Guderian, Manstein, and Executive Department Professor von Schneider looked grave.
“Thirteen students: twelve A-rank, one S-rank. Twenty-seven faculty. Everyone here,” Manstein told Schneider.
“Begin immediately.” Schneider wheeled his oxygen cylinder toward the wall and surveyed them. His fearsome face, half concealed by a black mask, quickly silenced the room.

“We need your help. Now. At this moment, two department members are trapped in dragon ruins. We obtained important material there, but triggered mechanisms have blocked their exit. Their oxygen diminishes every second. We must find a way out quickly.” Low and rapid, his voice suggested every second truly mattered.
“To find a route, you could use… Google Earth.” Lu Mingfei raised a hand. “Very… useful.”
Only after speaking did he realize how stupid it sounded. Everyone turned, looking as though they had seen a ghost.
“Google doesn’t cover places like this.” Schneider clapped. Ceiling-high teak shelves slid apart, revealing a gigantic hundred-inch screen.
A three-dimensional simulation appeared, scales along its edges. Everyone drew a sharp breath. A small… city cast in bronze!

“Norton’s palace. King of Bronze and Fire. Ancient ruins. Some of you descend from him. Here’s Draconic photographed by our agent Aki Sakatoku. We suspect it records the city’s casting. Concentrate and read it,” Schneider said.
“You hope one of us will resonate and enter spirit vision?” Caesar asked.
“Yes. Normally, deciphering this might take ten years. Their oxygen won’t last twenty minutes. Please hurry!”
“Aki Sakatoku?” Lu Mingfei remembered the Japanese interviewer with the girl-next-door manner. Her gentle smile. Was she in danger?
Everyone took laptops from their bags, Kiran and the girl included, plugged in data cables, and briskly swiped student cards through slots before them.
“Authorization granted… Authorization granted… Authorization granted…”
Norma’s voice echoed as students and professors entered their interfaces.
At the same time, photographs stitched together into a huge bronze-green dome on the screen. Lu Mingfei stared. This was Draconic? It was… a big tree!
“Dragons are all… artsy types, aren’t they?” He wanted to curse. Who did this? Invent a script without simplifying its rhetoric, use pictures to convey meaning—only an artsy type would do that!
“Swipe! There’s a spare computer,” Nono said nearby.
“Right!” He fished the card from his back pocket and fumbled it through.
The desktop opened, revealing a tablet. Its screen lit with a setup page. A three-dimensional girl appeared, in a long white gauze dress like a nightgown, hair floating, and bowed lightly.
“S-rank freshman Lu Mingfei. Delighted to assist. Please configure your system.” Her voice came through his headphones.
“Wow! Thoughtful beginner’s guide!” He was delighted. “Are you Norma? Thought you were a middle-aged lady.”
“I’m EVA.” She smiled. “Your record shows no computing courses. Shall I configure the standard setup?”
“No problem!” Anything a pretty girl said was good. Unless EVA made it look like StarCraft, he wouldn’t know how to use it anyway.
Windows flashed. The StarCraft interface appeared.
“More familiar?” EVA said. “Use this. Click to read, move, or save. You’ll learn quickly.”
He stared as the tree picture appeared in his map panel.
Aboard Moniach, Mans looked grim. “Still in contact? How long can they hold?”
“Ye Sheng’s Snakes maintain communications. No idea for how long. Yanling drains his strength and increases oxygen consumption.” Selma was pale. “Time’s running out.”
“Rescue helicopters sixty kilometers away!” the first officer shouted, removing his headphones.

“I think I understand the system Aki was lured into starting. Not a clock. The entire city is a machine! Once activated, bronze components move. Old routes close, new ones appear. A city like a Rubik’s Cube. But we have no map… Her photographs may be the map. None of us can read it!” Mans slammed a fist on the console.
“The principal ordered headquarters to help decipher it. All we can do is wait,” Selma said.

Lu Mingfei looked around. Everyone contemplated the picture, pencils whispering as they sketched. Caesar and Chu stared at the main screen, faces terribly dark. Kiran held his forehead in both hands. Nono stood with folded arms, brow deeply furrowed. The petite girl sat motionless as a statue.

The faculty argued fiercely in hushed voices. Their bloodlines were weaker than those of the top students. They couldn’t rely on spirit vision, but had studied Draconic for decades. They hoped to combine that knowledge into a miracle within twenty minutes.

He thought they were loyal, hardworking people. Extracting a map from a picture in twenty minutes was impossible. But they were elites. With even a sliver of hope, giving up was shameful. Like Spider-Man’s dying uncle saying, with great power comes great responsibility. Lu Mingfei was different: the bystander who screamed when the Green Goblin threw Mary Jane, Spider-Man’s girlfriend, from the sky. To others, Draconic sounded like thunder; its patterns came alive, flowering and growing leaves. For him, chanting was chanting, trees were trees. Plain and sturdy.
If—only if—he had the ability to think alongside these elites and save Ye Sheng and Aki, he would gladly rack his brains and give everything.
He rather liked handsome Ye Sheng and lovely Aki, despite their silly questions. What a waste if they died. Nono was right. Why didn’t they get married?

Seconds slipped away. He sighed. A rescue across the ocean was unrealistic. Some things were cruel. Like playing Zerg, with two Zerglings trapped inside a Terran base, tanks already deployed to bombard them. If you started hatching Mutalisks now, would you make it? Not a chance.
He paused, trembling slightly. Perhaps it wasn’t too late. A chance remained… Provided he was willing… to cheat!
A map… Wasn’t that simply revealing the map?
Black sheep wall!
Black Sheep. The restless, wicked member of a flock of white sheep. It was stirring.

He felt only a paper-thin barrier separated him from something forbidden. Here was a room of white sheep, penned behind walls, obediently grazing without looking out, destined to be grabbed and shorn. But black sheep… Black sheep jumped walls and escaped. A very, very bad boy who never played by the rules.
He furtively looked around and pressed Enter. Sure enough, a text box appeared.
“Black Sheep Wall.” Letter by letter, making sure not one was wrong.

Seconds later, every interface changed, going black. From top to bottom, a huge three-dimensional map refreshed. Everyone froze, hardly believing their eyes. The enormous bronze city was resolved into components, moving, sealing old passages and opening new ones.
Lu Mingze’s promise had become real. A miracle was happening. Lu Mingfei had jumped the wall, playing the mischievous black sheep.
Everyone whipped around to stare at him. Everyone recognized the correct answer. Clearly labeled in the map’s corner: LU MINGFEI’S DECIPHERMENT.
The ice-sculpture girl turned, too. For the first time, he saw her face, translucent as ice and snow.
